policy: Manually reviewed source content; not inferred from tags. Initial memberships cover the 20 preserved writeups; new reviewed metadata may extend this later.

topics.title: Web Security
topics.description: Lab walkthroughs covering authentication weaknesses, upload handling, exposed files and vulnerable web applications.
topics.intro: Start with [RootMe]({{ '/TryHackMe/RootMe.html' | relative_url }}#exploitation) for upload handling, then [Overpass]({{ '/TryHackMe/Overpass.html' | relative_url }}#2-initial-access) for client-side session handling. [Bricks Heist]({{ '/TryHackMe/TryHack3MBricksHeist.html' | relative_url }}#2-initial-access) follows a vulnerable WordPress theme into code execution.
members: An alternative PHP extension bypasses the upload filter.
The walkthrough changes a session cookie after inspecting client-side authentication logic.
Fuel CMS 1.4 remote code execution is investigated and used for initial access.
The walkthrough uses an elFinder PHP connector exploit after web authentication testing.
Authenticated WordPress file editing is used to execute a PHP shell.
An exposed CMS backup leads to access and PHP payload upload.
The writeup identifies and reproduces Bricks Builder CVE-2024-25600.
A writable SMB share maps to an IIS web root, enabling web-served payload execution.
The event highlights concurrent Burp requests used to test a coupon race condition.

topics.title: Linux Privilege Escalation
topics.description: Privilege boundaries in Linux labs: sudo rules, SUID programs, scheduled tasks, executable search paths and capabilities.
topics.intro: [RootMe]({{ '/TryHackMe/RootMe.html' | relative_url }}#3-priviledge-escalation) is a short SUID example. [Wonderland]({{ '/TryHackMe/wonderland.html' | relative_url }}#3-privilege-escalation) connects Python imports, executable search paths and capabilities; [Skynet]({{ '/TryHackMe/Skynet.html' | relative_url }}#4-root-flag) examines a wildcard-driven backup task.
members: A SUID Python interpreter provides the escalation path.
Python module hijacking, a SUID binary's PATH lookup and Perl capabilities are analyzed.
A scheduled script download is redirected through writable hostname resolution.
A privileged tar wildcard task is made to interpret attacker-controlled filenames as options.
A writable script is executed through a sudo-enabled Perl backup task.
A sudo-enabled backup script permits command execution through its arguments.
Sudo-permitted file reads expose protected password data.
A sudo-enabled zip invocation provides an escalation path.
The writeup inspects permitted sudo commands and uses them to cross a privilege boundary.

topics.title: Credential Attacks
topics.description: Credential discovery, password testing, cracking and reuse across FTP, SSH, web applications and exposed artifacts.
topics.intro: [Basic Pentesting]({{ '/TryHackMe/BasicPentesting.html' | relative_url }}#2-initial-access) connects SSH password testing with key-passphrase recovery. [Tomghost]({{ '/TryHackMe/Tomghost.html' | relative_url }}#pgp-credentials) follows encrypted artifacts, while [h4cked]({{ '/TryHackMe/h4cked.html' | relative_url }}#hydra-brute-force) connects observed FTP attempts with validation.
members: FTP password testing and embedded artifacts lead to further credentials.
The walkthrough tests SSH passwords and later cracks an SSH key passphrase.
Hydra is used to test SSH credentials.
A web form is tested with Hydra; the writeup also recovers a key passphrase.
An exposed password hash is cracked to access backup-related material.
An exposed SSH private key is converted for passphrase cracking.
Web error differences and password testing are followed by credential recovery and reuse.
John and PGP decryption are used to recover credentials from encrypted artifacts.
WordPress username discovery and dictionary-based login testing are documented.
FTP password attempts observed in traffic are validated with Hydra.
A packet capture exposes a password that is tested against another local account.
An SMB share exposes encoded credential material, decoded during enumeration.

topics.title: Enumeration
topics.description: Service discovery, web paths and SMB shares used to narrow an attack path before exploitation.
topics.intro: [Basic Pentesting]({{ '/TryHackMe/BasicPentesting.html' | relative_url }}#smb-enumeration) starts from shared files and usernames. [Relevant]({{ '/TryHackMe/Relevant.html' | relative_url }}#nmap-part-2) shows why scanning beyond default ports matters; [Bricks Heist]({{ '/TryHackMe/TryHack3MBricksHeist.html' | relative_url }}#wpscan-enumeration) adds application-specific inspection.
members: HTTP response behavior and FTP are investigated before initial access.
SMB shares and shared files reveal account information.
Web paths, dictionaries and WordPress login responses guide account discovery.
Full-port scanning and SMB enumeration identify an IIS/share relationship.
SMB files and successive web directory checks lead to the application attack path.
Web path discovery identifies the upload interface.
WPScan findings identify the outdated theme used in the subsequent attack.
Directory and homepage inspection establish the CMS version and login interface.

topics.title: Network Forensics
topics.description: Packet captures used to reconstruct activity, trace file transfers and recover evidence relevant to an attack path.
topics.intro: Start with [h4cked]({{ '/TryHackMe/h4cked.html' | relative_url }}#1-incident-discovery) for an FTP incident reconstruction in Wireshark. [Startup]({{ '/TryHackMe/Startup.html' | relative_url }}#3-user-flag) uses a capture found on the target to examine an earlier session.
members: Wireshark analysis reconstructs FTP login attempts, payload transfer and subsequent attacker activity.
The suspicious.pcapng capture is opened in Wireshark to recover the earlier attacker's commands and credential evidence.

topics.title: Reverse Engineering
topics.description: Debugger-guided inspection of compiled programs, branch decisions and executable behavior.
topics.intro: [Compiled]({{ '/TryHackMe/Compiled.html' | relative_url }}#2-buffer-overflow) works through GDB inspection and control-flow decisions. [Wonderland]({{ '/TryHackMe/wonderland.html' | relative_url }}#hatter-path-hijacking) examines how a binary invokes another executable and turns that observation into a testable path.
members: GDB/GEF inspection follows offsets, return addresses and conditional branches.
GDB inspection of the teaParty binary exposes an executable lookup that is later tested through PATH hijacking.
